extracted.intended_audience: inquiring readers, students, and researchers seeking bibliographies and histories of the American Civil War
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended works for reading and selecting reliable histories, memoirs, and bibliographies about the American Civil War. Emphasizes use of original evidence, specialist studies, and appropriate bibliographic supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base chronicle on original evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The present Chronicle is based entirely on the original evidence, with the convenient use only of such works as have themselves been written by qualified experts directly from the original evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer primary sources as the foundation for a chronicle; use secondary works only when those works were themselves produced by qualified experts who worked from original evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement older bibliographies with current bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Larned's Literature of American History contains an excellent bibliography; but it needs supplementing by bibliographies of the present century. Inquiring readers should consult the bibliographies in volumes 20 and 21 (by J. K. Hosmer) in the American Nation series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using established bibliographies, update them with more recent bibliographic guides (e.g., Hosmer's volumes) to capture works of the present century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value memoirs and first-person accounts by principal actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The two greatest generals on the Northern side have written their own memoirs, and written them exceedingly well: Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant ... and Memoirs of General W. T. Sherman ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoirs by principal participants (especially senior commanders) are often authoritative and well-written sources; however, recognize that not all leading figures or sides produced comparable memoirs and that later biographies may vary in quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match works to the reader's topical interest (military, political, naval)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: The first (Wood & Edmonds) is military, the second (James Ford Rhodes) political. The naval side has been neglected but Admiral Mahan's Admiral Farragut tells the best of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose histories according to their disciplinary focus—military campaigns, political/diplomatic history, or naval history—since single works may specialize in one aspect and differ substantially in approach and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary and pictorial accounts for vivid, graphic perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: An interesting contemporary account of the war will be found in the five volumes of Appleton's American Annual Cyclopædia for the years from 1861 to 1865. B. J. Lossing's Pictorial History of the Civil War ... and Harper's Pictorial History of the Rebellion ... give graphic pictures of military life as seen by contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To gain vivid, contemporary impressions of military life and events, consult contemporary annuals and pictorial histories, recognizing that these convey immediate visual and narrative perspectives distinct from later analytic histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appraise personal reminiscences cautiously; quality varies
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal reminiscences of the war, of varying merit, have multiplied rapidly in recent years. These are appraised for the unwary reader in the bibliographies already mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal recollections can provide valuable firsthand detail but vary widely in reliability and perspective; consult bibliographies and critical guides to evaluate their merit before relying on them as historical evidence.
